title: A Soundscape Under Strain
paragraphs: Human noise from shipping, road traffic, aircraft and other industrial activity now penetrates almost every habitat on Earth, and ambient sound levels in the oceans are estimated to be around ten times higher than they were in 1950. A meta-analysis published in Science this month, which pooled 214 experimental studies of 177 aquatic and terrestrial species across six continents, concluded that noise altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in four out of five of the species examined, with effects appearing in every type of habitat. Its authors report that predators working in noisy conditions must expend roughly two and a half times more effort to catch about a quarter fewer prey, while engine noise from ships disrupts communication and disorientates marine mammals such as whales and dolphins.

The consequences extend beyond individual animals. Many species simply abandon noisy places, which shrinks the area available to them and therefore caps the size of their populations; dolphins shun noisy coastlines, and bats have been observed avoiding roads that were loud during a motorcycle rally long after the vehicles had departed. Across the animals studied, mortality in noise-affected areas rose by 138 per cent on average, sometimes abruptly, as when underwater explosions rupture a fish's bladder, and sometimes slowly, through starvation caused by poorer hunting. Hansjoerg Kunc, one of the researchers, concedes that not every animal loses out, since certain predators gain temporarily when noise flushes prey from cover. He regards that as beside the point, however: an ecosystem whose species have adapted to one acoustic environment is being distorted by an external stressor, and he argues that conservation should protect the natural soundscape alongside physical habitat.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Human noise harms animals chiefly in the oceans, because sound levels at sea have risen about tenfold since 1950.
Human noise affects animals across habitats, because it alters their behaviour, shrinks their living space and raises mortality.
Human noise affects animals through stress alone, because the harm it causes is physiological and not behavioural or developmental.
Human noise harms animals that stay in noisy places, because species that leave spare their populations any damage at all.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does avoiding noisy places reduce the size of a species' population?

options.text: It disrupts breeding, so fewer young survive to adulthood in the places where the animals remain.
It exposes them to more predators, which raises the death rate among the animals that stay behind.
It makes the animals spend more energy searching for food, which weakens them and shortens their lives.
Animals that leave noisy areas lose part of their range, which limits how many of them can be sustained.

questions.prompt: What is Kunc's attitude towards predators that benefit from noise?

options.text: He believes their gains show that noise pollution can sometimes benefit an ecosystem.
He considers their gains irrelevant to the wider disturbance of the ecosystem.
He argues that such predators should be studied separately from the species they hunt.
He suggests that their success is likely to outlast the harm done to their prey.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, 'pooled' is closest in meaning to

options.text: repeated the findings of
randomly selected from
combined the results of
disagreed with

title: One Gene, Many Questions
paragraphs: Autism is diagnosed less often in women and girls, and researchers have now pointed to a single gene on the X chromosome, ZFX, as a possible contributor to that gap. Females carry two X chromosomes and, unusually for X-linked genes, express both copies of ZFX, so they produce more of it than males do; the gene appears to keep other autism-associated genes switched on when they might otherwise be silenced. The widely quoted claim that autism is up to four times as common in males is contested, partly because autism presents differently in females and because many girls and women mask their traits, which delays diagnosis or prevents it altogether. Nevertheless, many specialists accept the existence of a female protective effect, and women who are diagnosed tend to carry more autism-linked mutations than diagnosed men, implying that females need a heavier genetic load before the condition becomes apparent.

To investigate, Rebecca Andersen's team grew neural progenitor cells in culture and used a gene-editing tool to degrade the RNA from 20 genes known to be linked to autism. Reducing any one of these genes usually lowered the activity of most of the others, a degree of convergence the researchers said they had not expected. A model of the interactions then identified a core of 70 genes that strongly regulate the 20 and one another, and, among genes more active in female brains, pointed to ZFX. If ZFX acts as a genetic buffer, a girl could inherit many variants that reduce the expression of autism-associated genes and yet be protected because ZFX raises it again. An independent expert called the idea biologically plausible, but cautioned that it rests on the model, that nobody has demonstrated that boosting ZFX rescues the effects of such variants, and that a protective effect this complex is unlikely to trace back to one gene alone.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: A gene on the X chromosome may explain the lower diagnosis rate in females, since it is more active in them and keeps other autism-linked genes switched on.
A gene on the X chromosome may explain the lower diagnosis rate in females, since it is less active in them, which lets other autism-linked genes be silenced.
A gene on the X chromosome may explain the lower diagnosis rate in females, since editing it in cultured cells showed that autism can be prevented.
A gene on the X chromosome may explain the lower diagnosis rate in females, since males who carry it are diagnosed only after years of masking.

questions.prompt: What does the finding that diagnosed women carry more autism-linked mutations than diagnosed men suggest?

options.text: Women may be more likely than men to inherit such mutations from their mothers rather than their fathers.
Such mutations may be less harmful to men than they are to women, whatever their number.
Many men who carry such mutations may never be diagnosed, because autism goes unrecognised in them.
Females may tolerate a greater number of such mutations before the condition becomes noticeable.

questions.prompt: In the second paragraph, 'convergence' refers to

options.text: the speed at which the gene-editing tool managed to degrade the targeted RNA
the similarity between the cultured cells and the cells of the human brain
the extent to which the activity of the genes proved interdependent
the way in which neural progenitor cells develop into mature neurons

questions.prompt: What does the independent expert's final comment imply about the ZFX hypothesis?

options.text: It has been confirmed by experiments in which ZFX activity was increased.
It is unlikely to be relevant to the way autism develops in females.
It undermines the model, since an effect this complex could not be traced to ZFX at all.
It is plausible but still rests on a model that has not been tested directly.

title: A Hiss to Help the Sleeping Brain
paragraphs: Brief bursts of pink noise, a low-pitched hiss, played during sleep might give people with early-stage Alzheimer's disease a slight memory boost, according to a small study of 37 participants who had been diagnosed with the disease and had mild cognitive impairment affecting memory. There is some evidence that exposure to pink noise during sleep may help clear waste products from the brain, and the researchers reasoned that it could also support the consolidation of memories, a process that Alzheimer's can disrupt and that relies on slow brainwaves and short bursts of neural activity.

On two evenings fourteen days apart, the volunteers came to the laboratory, memorised 30 word pairs and slept there while their brain activity was monitored. On the first night, a system designed by a Spanish neurotechnology company detected when slow brainwaves were about to peak and triggered a 50-millisecond pulse of pink noise each time; on the second night no noise was played. The timing matters, according to team member Javier Minguez, because the useful window is only about 200 milliseconds wide. After each night the participants tried to recall the pairs, and they remembered 0.88 more pairs, on average, after the night with pink noise, which the researchers equate to an improvement of about 19 per cent. They stress, however, that the clinical significance remains uncertain, and they disclose that several authors have commercial links to the company or its spin-off and that three are inventors on a pending patent covering the method.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Pink noise has improved memory in people with Alzheimer's, which means that it clears waste products from their brains during sleep.
Pink noise timed to brainwaves improved recall slightly in early Alzheimer's, which means the gain is small and of unclear importance.
Pink noise has improved recall in a large trial, which means that its benefit holds for healthy older adults as well as patients.
Pink noise improved recall on the night it was played, which means that continuous exposure works as well as timed pulses would.

questions.prompt: Why does the timing of each pulse matter, according to Minguez?

options.text: Longer pulses would wake the sleeping participants and spoil the experiment.
The noise can only help during a very brief period of about a fifth of a second.
The system can only detect slow brainwaves when they are at their lowest point.
Participants could not memorise the word pairs until the noise had stopped.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, 'reasoned' is closest in meaning to

options.text: argued on the basis of existing evidence
demonstrated in earlier experiments
admitted with some reluctance
doubted for lack of evidence

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the final sentences of the passage?

options.text: The company's method has proved effective enough to be offered to hospitals straight away, as the data stand.
The pending patent is likely to stop other research teams from repeating the experiment themselves.
The reported gain is of uncertain importance, and the authors' ties to the company call for care.
The authors' ties to the company mean that the memory gain was probably exaggerated in the study.

title: The Electrification Target
paragraphs: One of the main items under discussion at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya is a voluntary global target of raising electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035. The target is based on analysis by the International Energy Agency and the International Renewable Energy Agency of what is needed to keep the 1.5C warming limit within reach, and it has attracted at least 14 explicit endorsements, among them Australia, Germany and Norway, whereas the UK and the EU have acknowledged the need for electrification without formally backing the pledge. Some developing countries, such as Fiji, welcomed the idea but stressed that support would be required to deliver it.

Meeting it will be demanding. Electricity currently accounts for an estimated 23.4 per cent of the energy delivered to consumers, a share that has risen by only 6.7 percentage points since 2000, so the rate of electrification would have to quadruple compared with the first quarter of the century and triple compared with the years from 2020 to 2025. Judit Hecke of the German think tank New Climate Institute considers such an acceleration possible, but says the challenge lies in getting policies, investment and infrastructure to move at the same pace. Renewable energy offers encouragement: in 2024, nearly 32 per cent of global electricity came from renewable sources, against 18 per cent in 2000, and capacity has grown from 0.8 to 5.2 terawatts. Hecke points out, however, that the target counts electricity however it is generated, so a country could make progress while still relying heavily on coal and gas, and she argues that electrification, renewables and energy efficiency must be pursued together.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: The electrification target is demanding but feasible, because it needs a much faster pace and attention to how electricity is generated.
The electrification target is demanding but unlikely to matter, because only a limited number of countries have formally endorsed the pledge.
The electrification target is demanding and out of reach, because renewable growth has slowed since 2000 while coal and gas remain dominant.
The electrification target is demanding and divisive, because developing countries such as Fiji have made their support depend on funding.

questions.prompt: Why does Hecke say the target alone is not enough?

options.text: Much of the energy that consumers use cannot realistically be replaced by electricity, however fast the target is pursued.
It applies only to the countries that have already endorsed the pledge, leaving the largest emitters outside it.
It measures how far energy use is electrified without asking how the electricity is made, so fossil fuels could remain central.
It ignores how expensive renewable capacity remains in poorer countries, which will therefore struggle to meet it.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, 'endorsements' is closest in meaning to

options.text: binding legal obligations
financial contributions
formal objections
public statements of support

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the comparison with the year 2000?

options.text: Electrification has been moving faster than renewable power generation.
The 35 per cent target will be reached by continuing the existing trend.
Past progress is too slow to reach the target without a large acceleration.
Most of the increase in electricity's share came from renewable sources.

title: A Blood Thinner for Painful Knees
paragraphs: A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis, and the approach appears to work partly by dampening inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage. Osteoarthritis results from the wear and tear of the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, which leads to inflammation, pain and stiffness; painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can ease the symptoms, but no approved drug halts or slows the worsening of the condition. Two inflammatory molecules, TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta, are widely thought to drive that inflammation, yet trials of drugs aimed at either one have failed, possibly because the molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues.

To test whether targeting both would work better, the team surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knees of eight monkeys; a month later four of them began to receive a daily dose of dabigatran, a drug commonly used to prevent clots in people at risk of stroke that also blocks signalling through both molecules. Seven months on, scans showed that the cartilage in the treated monkeys was about 60 per cent thicker on average, and their left knees had roughly 15 per cent more range of motion than those of the controls. Experiments in mice gave similar results. Outside experts were encouraging but careful: Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford said a small clinical trial would be worth considering if another group replicated the findings, and she noted that some of the benefit might come from the drug's anti-clotting rather than its anti-inflammatory action. Because reducing clotting raises the risk of bleeding, Liu's team is now developing drugs that hit the two molecules without affecting clotting.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: A clot-preventing drug has relieved osteoarthritis in patients, which explains why researchers now want larger trials.
A clot-preventing drug has worked where earlier treatments failed, which shows that targeting one inflammatory molecule is enough.
A clot-preventing drug has improved knee cartilage in animals, though its mechanism and relevance to patients are unsettled.
A clot-preventing drug has caused bleeding in animals, which explains why researchers are now seeking safer alternatives.

questions.prompt: According to the researchers, why may earlier trials of drugs aimed at one molecule have failed?

options.text: If one molecule is blocked, the other may take over its role.
The drugs were given too late to affect cartilage that had already worn away.
The drugs relieved pain but increased inflammation in the knee.
Inflammation in osteoarthritis is caused mainly by blood clots rather than by molecules.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, 'wear and tear' is closest in meaning to

options.text: sudden injury caused by a heavy impact
gradual damage caused by long use
natural growth that occurs with age
repair after an earlier injury

questions.prompt: What does Vincent's comment suggest?

options.text: Part of the benefit may come from an effect other than the proposed one.
The monkey results are certain to be repeated in human patients in clinical trials.
A small clinical trial should be started before any further experiments.
The drug's effect on blood clotting is irrelevant to its action on the knee.

title: Opening the Door Without the Key
paragraphs: Psychedelics such as psilocybin, ketamine and LSD are increasingly regarded as remarkably effective treatments for serious mental illness, yet how they work remains unclear. Their benefit might reside in the radical disruption of brain chemistry and neural firing patterns, in the overwhelming experience of the trip, in the therapy that gives it meaning, or in some combination of the three. Most attempts to disentangle these possibilities have so far concentrated on engineering analogues that omit the trip yet, in mice, appear to reproduce some of the drugs' effects on neurons.

A growing minority of neuroscientists, among them Nicco Reggente at the University of California, Los Angeles, are exploring the converse hypothesis: that the therapeutic value derives from an intense alteration of perception, which upends a person's sense of self and of their place in the world. If so, drugs may be dispensable whenever other means can shake up the mental snow globe and let it settle into a healthier arrangement; psychedelics would merely be particularly good at picking the lock of a door that has other keys. Such alternatives have a long pedigree. Holotropic breathwork, a form of deliberate hyperventilation, was devised in the 1970s after psychedelic drugs were outlawed, and meditation and sensory deprivation can also transform mental states. Interest in these methods grew out of the psychedelic research of the 1950s and 1960s, but waned as Prozac and other antidepressants arrived and mental health research moved on.

With many obstacles to the clinical use of psychedelics unresolved, drug-free approaches have returned to the agenda, this time with technology as a central component. The best studied is stroboscopic light stimulation, in which rapidly flashing lights beamed onto closed eyelids generate vivid visual hallucinations within seconds, without the training that meditation or breathing practices require. In a 2024 study of 262 people, the technique reduced anxiety and improved mood as effectively as breath-focused meditation, and did so in just over five minutes rather than ten. One proposed explanation is predictive processing, the theory that the brain builds its picture of the self and the world by generating predictions from past experience and comparing them with incoming sensory information; colours that move in unexpected ways would then undermine the implicit confidence that the world is as it habitually appears, potentially opening the mind to change.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Researchers have shown that brain chemistry is the source of the benefits, because analogues that omit the trip reproduce some of the drugs' effects in mice.
Researchers have shown that therapy is the source of the benefits, because it gives the experience its meaning.
Researchers have proposed that altered perception is the source of the benefits, which would make drug-free ways of inducing it worth testing.
Researchers have shown that drug-free methods work better than the drugs, because meditation and breathwork predate the research on psychedelics.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is closest in meaning to 'psychedelics would merely be particularly good at picking the lock of a door that has other keys'?

options.text: Psychedelics are an especially effective but replaceable way of reaching a state that other methods can also produce.
Psychedelics are the quickest of several routes to a state that the other methods can only partly approximate.
Psychedelics are effective only because they open a door that the other methods have already unlocked for them.
Psychedelics are a forceful but unreliable way of reaching a state that the other methods reach more gently.

questions.prompt: How does Reggente's hypothesis relate to the approach that most earlier studies have taken?

options.text: It reverses it: most studies keep the drugs' neural effects and drop the experience, while the minority keep the experience and question the drug.
It extends it: both groups try to reproduce the drugs' effects on neurons, but the minority do so with technology rather than with analogues.
It contradicts it: the minority deny that the trip has any therapeutic role and concentrate on therapy as the only active ingredient.
It confirms it: the minority treat the engineered analogues in mice as proof that altered perception is what drives the benefit.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by the final paragraph?

options.text: Flashing lights may produce an effect comparable to that of meditation, and may do so more quickly.
The 2024 study found no advantage for meditation over the light technique in reducing anxiety.
Predictive processing is offered as a possible explanation of the effect, not as an established mechanism.
The 2024 study showed that flashing lights alter a person's sense of self just as psychedelic drugs do.

title: A Clock Timed by the Sun
paragraphs: Optical clocks, the most precise timekeepers ever built, normally owe their accuracy to atoms isolated from the outside world: an electron inside an atom is made to oscillate between two energy levels, an ultra-stable laser is locked to the frequency of that oscillation, and a device called a frequency comb converts the rapid light waves into microwaves that ordinary electronics can count as ticks. Researchers led by Scott Diddams at the University of Colorado, Boulder, have now built a version in which the atomic reference is replaced by something that occurs at the sun itself.

Instead of locking their laser to an electron's jumps inside a laboratory atom, the team locked it to a process in which sunlight causes comparable jumps as it strikes iron atoms in the solar atmosphere. That process leaves a signature in the spectrum of colours that make up sunlight, so the researchers channelled sunlight into a special fibre and fed it into the rest of the apparatus. A clock of this kind has never been constructed before. It does not rival the best atomic optical clocks in accuracy, but during the partial solar eclipse of 2024 the team observed a characteristic shift in the spectrum as the moon passed in front of the sun, which suggests that such a device could serve as a tool for studying stars.

Fed with light from a distant star, the same design might indicate the presence of orbiting exoplanets through similar shifts, although starlight would have to be gathered by large telescopes, sometimes over long periods. Piet Schmidt, of the National Metrology Institute of Germany, welcomed the work because it draws on light from the stars rather than on objects kept under tight laboratory control, yet he cautioned that as an astronomical instrument it does not yet surpass existing methods, and that for very faint, distant stars its usefulness would be severely limited. He sees better prospects closer to home, where the clock might probe eruptions, sunspots and the solar wind in the outer layers of the sun's atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: A clock referenced to the sun has matched laboratory clocks, because sunlight replaces the laser that normally sets the reference frequency.
A clock referenced to the sun has found exoplanets, because the 2024 eclipse produced the same spectral shift that orbiting planets cause.
A clock referenced to the sun has replaced the frequency comb, because sunlight can be counted directly by ordinary electronics.
A clock referenced to the sun is less accurate than laboratory clocks, but shifts in its sunlight suggest uses in astronomy.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the reference to the partial solar eclipse of 2024?

options.text: To demonstrate that the clock keeps accurate time even when part of the sunlight is blocked from reaching it.
To show that the spectral change the clock relies on can be seen to vary, which hints at uses in astronomy.
To explain why the clock outperforms atomic optical clocks whenever the light it receives is changing.
To justify the need for large telescopes, which must gather light for long periods before any shift can be seen.

questions.prompt: How far does Schmidt's approval of the new clock extend?

options.text: He endorses the clock as a replacement for current astronomical instruments, provided that starlight is gathered by large telescopes.
He endorses the principle behind the design, but expects it to prove useless outside the laboratory.
He endorses its practical performance, while questioning whether sunlight can serve as a reference at all.
He endorses the idea of drawing on natural light, while limiting its practical value to the nearby sun rather than distant stars.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is closest in meaning to the statement that the design 'draws on light from the stars rather than on objects kept under tight laboratory control'?

options.text: Its reference comes from natural light arriving from space, not from specially prepared and controlled laboratory systems.
Its light comes from stars because laboratory objects cannot be controlled tightly enough to serve as a reference.
Its accuracy comes from starlight being steadier than any object that can be held under laboratory control.
Its design uses stars only to check the readings of a clock that is otherwise built and controlled in a laboratory.

title: Economics, Not Summits
paragraphs: The hosts of the COP31 summit, Turkey and Australia, are urging a clean energy revolution while expanding fossil fuel production: Turkey has announced two new oilfields and a plan to double natural gas output, and Australia has approved projects that include a coal mine extension that critics call a climate bomb. Collective climate action has effectively stalled since the 2015 Paris Agreement, which nevertheless shaved more than 1C off the projected warming trajectory, and current policies still point towards a rise of about 2.7C by 2100, according to Climate Action Tracker. There is one encouraging sign: the Global Carbon Budget expects fossil fuel emissions to fall slightly in 2026, by 0.4 per cent, although that drop would not have occurred without the oil price spike caused by the Iran war.

The central argument is that economics, rather than diplomacy, is now driving the transition. Solar generates ten times more energy than when the Paris deal was signed, making it the fastest-growing source of electricity ever, and electricity from solar and wind costs less on average than electricity from gas or coal. Auke Hoekstra of Eindhoven University of Technology contends that policy was never the main driver, because the technologies are simply superior; Texas, the leading oil-producing state, has become the leading producer of solar and wind power, and in Nigeria and Pakistan households are installing cheap Chinese panels instead of waiting for governments to upgrade unreliable fossil-fuelled grids. Cheap batteries are solving the remaining drawback, that solar and wind produce little energy during evening peak demand.

Policy still matters, however, since early subsidies and regulations in China and Germany created the conditions for renewables to fall down the cost curve, and governments continue to provide more than 900 billion dollars a year in support for fossil fuels. Expanding the grid is the biggest bottleneck, something governments could speed up by cutting red tape and offering subsidies and loans. Kingsmill Bond of the think tank Ember Energy believes that the economics of clean technology will allow the world to limit warming to well below 2.7C, with the exact outcome depending on politics, and he proposes that energy-importing countries convene their own COP in which fossil fuel exporters cannot delay progress.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Climate summits have driven the energy transition, because the Paris Agreement lowered projected warming by more than 1C.
Cheap solar power has made government policy irrelevant, because Texas and Nigeria show households adopting it without state help.
Fossil fuel emissions are now falling steadily, because costs have dropped and governments have ended subsidies for fossil fuels.
Falling technology costs are driving the transition ahead of diplomacy, though policy still shapes how fast it can go.

questions.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the expected fall in fossil fuel emissions in 2026?

options.text: It is better read as the product of a one-off price shock than as a sign that climate policy is working.
It reflects tougher emissions targets that governments agreed at earlier climate summits.
It shows that falling solar and wind costs have finally begun to outweigh the growth in fossil fuel use.
It will probably continue each year for as long as clean energy remains cheaper than gas and coal.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by the second paragraph?

options.text: Governments in oil-producing regions have encouraged the spread of solar and wind through generous new subsidies.
Cost advantages can lead households to adopt solar power even where their governments are slow to act.
The expansion of solar and wind in Texas suggests that fossil fuels and renewables can grow side by side.
Cheap batteries address a remaining weakness of solar and wind, namely their low output during evening peak demand.

questions.prompt: What does Bond's proposal most strongly imply about the current climate negotiations?

options.text: They are dominated by importing countries that have little to lose from a faster transition away from fossil fuels.
They have already delivered the policies needed to keep warming well below 2.7C by the end of the century.
They allow countries that export fossil fuels to slow progress, in a way that the proposed new forum would prevent.
They have no bearing on the transition, since market forces alone determine how quickly it proceeds.
